conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for making time today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS, with you. It’s a quick, well-studied set of questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, so please answer as openly as you feel comfortable.

We’ll go through 10 short questions about the past seven days. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to over-think, just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly? It’s been pretty hard to laugh lately. When my partner tries to make a joke or when I scroll past something that used to crack me up, it just feels flat. I might give a half-smile, but I can’t remember the last time I really laughed—at least not since the baby came.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. My sister sent me one of those silly animal videos we used to howl over, and I just stared at it. It’s like the “funny” part of me is switched off right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a shower without interruptions—but lately it all feels like one more task. I don’t really look forward to anything. I just hope I’ll get through the day without feeling completely drained.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his sleepy cue. Yesterday I dropped a burp cloth on the floor and burst into tears because I couldn’t even manage that. I know it sounds small, but in my head it feels like proof I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all day, every day. Even when he’s napping I’m tiptoeing in to check he’s breathing, or scrolling online about fevers and rashes. My heart races over things that probably won’t happen—like what if I trip while holding him, or what if I sleep too hard and don’t hear him cry? I can’t seem to turn the “what-ifs” off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, I get those sudden waves—like when I’m just sitting on the couch feeding him, and out of nowhere my chest tightens and I feel like I can’t get enough air. It’s like my body’s sounding an alarm, but there’s no real danger. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky and watching the door, half-expecting something awful to burst in.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m treading water: the moment I finish one feed, the next is due, the laundry’s still piled up, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep telling myself other moms manage, so why can’t I get it together? I get through, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above the surface.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I lie down exhausted, but my brain just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles, is he breathing, am I doing any of this right? Some nights I fall asleep okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t drift off again. I end up staring at the ceiling feeling this heavy sadness settle in until I hear him stir and the whole cycle starts over.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most of my days. I’ll be changing his diaper and tears just start leaking out—I couldn’t tell you exactly why. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me that won’t budge. I keep waiting to feel that little lift, even for an hour, but it hasn’t come.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... at least three or four times this week. Sometimes it's because I'm overwhelmed—like when he won't latch and the clock says he's been nursing for an hour—but other times it just hits out of nowhere. Yesterday I cried in the shower for ten minutes, no real trigger, just this heavy sadness spilling out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

You have shared that since your baby arrived laughter and excitement feel out of reach, daily tasks loom like mountains, and a heavy sadness follows you even into the shower. You tear up without warning, blame yourself for every hiccup in your baby's care, and live with constant worry and sudden panic that leave you shaky and breathless. Yet you have also clearly stated you have no thoughts of harming yourself, and you came here today seeking support-both powerful protective factors.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports total inability to laugh or find anything funny, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing all activities as burdensome tasks rather than sources of enjoyment.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for everyday infant care issues, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, and physiologically intense worry throughout the day without real triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms (chest tightness, shortness of breath) that occur frequently and without warning, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes feeling persistently overwhelmed and struggling to keep up with daily tasks, which aligns with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent sleep disruption from unhappiness—initial insomnia, middle-of-the-night waking, and racing thoughts—matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of my days" with uncontrollable crying and persistent low mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying multiple times per week with both situational and spontaneous episodes, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the EPDS threshold of 14 that flags probable major depression. You endorse five core symptoms consistent with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, recurrent anxiety and panic, and sleep disturbance. The combination of daily crying, self-blame over small missteps, and inability to feel joy indicates moderate-severe symptom intensity. Although you deny self-harm, functional impairment is significant as you describe barely keeping your head above water while caring for your infant. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, short-term <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline (<med>SSRI</med>) compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
4. Mobilize support: partner or friend to handle one night feeding, and accept prepared meals so you can rest
5. Practice brief self-care-five-minute outdoor step or shower while support person holds baby-to reduce sensory overload
6. Keep crisis resources handy: 24-hr Postpartum Support International helpline, local emergency department if thoughts of self-harm ever emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 0–4 mo post-delivery, self-report on EPDS-equivalent 10-item query.

Areas endorsed (moderate–severe range):
- Anhedonia: marked loss of humor & anticipatory pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting competence (Q3)  
- Generalized & postpartum-specific anxiety, panic surges with physical symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, “treading water,” feels unable to cope (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (onset & maintenance) (Q7)

Safety: Denies self-harm thoughts (Q10); no suicidal ideation elicited.

Pattern: Symptoms pervasive, present most days, causing functional impairment with infant care; no discrete high-risk behaviors reported.

Screening significance: High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety in postpartum context; warrants prompt formal evaluation and possible referral to perinatal mental health specialty.
